text: {"foundGenuineWeakness":true,"weaknessDescription":"The lead evidence is a remote-sensing product, and using it here conflates instrument detection with unaided human vision. Three specific problems. (1) Wrong instrument: ASTER resolves roughly 15 m per pixel from orbit; the human eye at the same distance does not, so the image establishes that a sensor can distinguish the structure, which is a different proposition from whether an eye can. (2) Selected conditions: the caption itself states the detection depended on a low sun angle and light snow cover, i.e. transient conditions that manufacture edge contrast the structure does not ordinarily have against same-coloured terrain. Evidence gathered under conditions chosen because they maximise the effect cannot be read as evidence about ordinary conditions. (3) Unverified identification: a single 12 x 12 km sub-image is reported as showing the Wall as a black line, with no independent check that the linear feature is the Wall rather than a road, a field boundary, or a ridge shadow, all of which are common in that terrain and would look the same at this resolution. Separately, this origin was selected as the lead only because it carries the highest warrant grade; on the substance it does not bear on unaided visibility at all."}

text: {"foundGenuineWeakness":true,"weaknessDescription":"The calculation may apply the wrong psychophysical criterion, which is a real objection and not a quibble. Visual acuity as used here is a MINIMUM-ANGLE-OF-RESOLUTION measure: the angular separation at which two features are told apart, calibrated on gap-detection targets such as Landolt rings. Detecting the presence of a long, high-contrast linear feature against a contrasting background is a different task with a different and much finer threshold, which is why power lines, contrails and roads are readily seen at distances where their angular width is far below the acuity limit the paper invokes. If line detection rather than two-point resolution is the governing threshold, the derived requirement of roughly 20/3 overstates what the observation would actually demand, and the argument does not go through as stated. Two further gaps. The contrast assumption is generic, whereas the conditions under which the structure is reported as distinguishable are precisely the atypical high-contrast ones, low sun angle and snow outlining the wall, which the model does not treat. And the headline figure and the boundary case are computed at different distances, ISS altitude for one and about 80 km for the other, so they are not directly comparable. None of this shows the conclusion is wrong; the structure is genuinely narrow and genuinely the colour of its surroundings. It shows this particular derivation rests on a criterion choice the source never defends, and a peer-reviewed paper arguing the opposite conclusion on exactly that ground exists and could not be retrieved in this run."}
